summary.text: The third law of thermodynamics says that a system's entropy approaches a constant value as its temperature approaches absolute zero.
For a perfect crystal of a pure substance that constant is zero, because at minimum energy there is a single unique arrangement of its atoms.
A consequence is that no process can reach absolute zero in a finite number of steps, and the law gives an absolute reference point for measuring entropy.

facts.label: Glassy systems
facts.value: Can keep some residual entropy at very low temperatures

facts.label: Reaching zero
facts.value: Impossible in a finite number of operations

facts.label: Crystal defects
facts.value: Some crystals form defects that leave residual entropy

items.prompt: A flawless crystal of a pure substance is cooled toward absolute zero. What happens to its entropy?

options.label: It rises to a large fixed value
It stays the same as at room temperature
It drops toward zero
It grows without limit

items.explain: The entropy of a perfect crystal of a pure substance approaches zero as the temperature approaches zero.

items.prompt: A sample of glass is cooled to nearly absolute zero, yet some disorder remains. Why?

options.label: It lacks a well-defined order, so a leftover entropy can remain
Glass cannot lose any heat once it is solid
Cooling adds disorder after a certain point
Glass is a gas that has not finished condensing

items.explain: Without well-defined order the system can lock into a non-minimal energy configuration, or have a non-unique lowest state, leaving a residual entropy.

items.prompt: A team plans to chill a sample to exactly zero kelvin by adding enough cooling stages. What does the third law say?

options.label: It works if the pressure is high enough
It works with enough stages, in finite time
It cannot be done in any finite number of steps
It works only if done without heat exchange

items.explain: No process can bring a system to absolute zero in a finite number of operations; it would take infinitely many steps or infinite time.

items.prompt: Why is the entropy of a perfect crystal exactly zero at absolute zero?

options.label: All of its atoms have left the crystal
It has only one lowest-energy arrangement
Entropy cannot be measured in a crystal
Its atoms vibrate faster than anywhere else

items.explain: Entropy relates to the number of accessible microstates; with one unique minimum-energy state, the entropy at absolute zero is zero.

items.prompt: Why can scientists quote an absolute entropy for a substance rather than only entropy changes?

options.label: Because entropy is always measured at room temperature
Because entropy never changes in a closed system
Because heat capacity is infinite at low temperatures
Because the law supplies a fixed zero point to measure from

items.explain: The third law gives an absolute reference point, so entropy of a closed system measured from it is its absolute entropy.

items.prompt: Someone squeezes a sample harder before cooling it. Will the entropy it approaches at absolute zero change?

options.label: Yes, it rises with more squeezing
Yes, it falls with more squeezing
No, the constant does not depend on such parameters
No, but only if the sample is a gas

items.explain: The constant value cannot depend on other parameters of the system, such as pressure or an applied magnetic field.

paragraphs.heading: What the law says
paragraphs.text: The third law of thermodynamics is about what happens to entropy as a system is cooled toward absolute zero, or zero kelvin. As the temperature drops toward that limit, the entropy of a closed system in equilibrium settles to a constant value. That value cannot depend on anything else about the system, such as the pressure on it or a magnetic field applied to it. At absolute zero itself, the system must sit in its lowest possible energy state.

paragraphs.heading: Why the value is often zero
paragraphs.text: Entropy is tied to the number of microstates a system can reach, meaning the detailed arrangements that fit its large-scale condition. Usually just one state has the lowest energy, and it is called the ground state. In that case the entropy at absolute zero is exactly zero, since the entropy then depends only on how many ground states there are. A perfect crystal of a pure substance is the standard case: its neat alignment leaves no doubt where each part sits or which way it points. As its energy falls, the vibrations of its atoms die away until the crystal is the same everywhere.

paragraphs.heading: Leftover entropy
paragraphs.text: Not every system ends up perfectly ordered. A glassy material may keep some entropy at very low temperature, either because it gets stuck in an arrangement that is not the lowest in energy or because more than one lowest-energy state exists. This leftover amount is called residual entropy. Some crystals form defects that cause it, and it vanishes once the kinetic barriers blocking the move to a single ground state are overcome. Glasses and solid solutions keep a lot of entropy at 0 K because they are trapped among a great many states of nearly equal energy.

paragraphs.heading: Absolute zero is out of reach
paragraphs.text: The chemist Walther Nernst developed the law between 1906 and 1912, so it is often called the Nernst heat theorem. One of its forms is about cooling: no process, however idealized, can lower a system's entropy all the way to its value at absolute zero using only finitely many operations. Reaching absolute zero would therefore take endless steps or endless time. In 1912 Nernst himself wrote that no procedure can get to the isotherm T = 0 within finitely many steps.

paragraphs.heading: A zero point for entropy
paragraphs.text: The law gives entropy a fixed reference point from which it can be found at any other temperature. Entropy measured from this zero point is called the system's absolute entropy. In mathematical terms, absolute entropy at zero temperature is the natural log of how many ground states there are, multiplied by k_B, the Boltzmann constant, whose value is 1.38×10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. The starting value S₀ could be any number as long as every calculation uses the same one, so S₀ = 0 is chosen for convenience.

paragraphs.heading: One photon in a crystal
paragraphs.text: Picture a crystal of N identical atoms at 0 K, met by a single incoming photon. At first only one microstate is available, so S₀ = k_Bln Ω = k_Bln 1 = 0. Suppose one atom absorbs the photon. Afterwards the system has N possible microstates, one for each atom that might be the excited one while the rest stay in the ground state. Only one atom takes in the photon, yet the change in temperature and entropy belongs to the whole system.

paragraphs.heading: Systems without one ground state
paragraphs.text: Some systems never have a single ground state. If a system's net spin is a half-integer, time-reversal symmetry gives it two ground states of equal energy, so its entropy at zero temperature is no less than k_B ln(2), a tiny amount on everyday scales. In some crystals, geometrical frustration means the shape of the lattice stops a unique ground state from forming. And helium in its ground state stays liquid unless it is put under pressure.
